explanation: At the least significant bit, a complete consecutive range has as many zeros as ones or one extra zero. Removing a zero leaves zero-count no larger than one-count; removing a one leaves more zeros. This identifies the missing low bit without reconstructing any number. Retain only indices with that bit, discard the known low bit conceptually, and repeat. Each retained set shrinks by roughly half.
correctness: At each stage the candidate values share the already determined low-bit prefix. Shifting away that prefix gives a consecutive range starting at zero with exactly the shifted missing value absent. Its even positions are either equal in count to its odd positions or one greater before removal. Therefore observed zeroCount<=oneCount identifies a missing zero bit, and the opposite inequality identifies a missing one bit. Keeping the selected partition preserves the consecutive-range-with-one-missing invariant for the next higher bit. When no candidates remain, the shifted complete range is {0}, so all remaining missing bits are zero. Accumulating the selected bits returns exactly the omitted integer. The geometric partition sizes give linear total bit queries, within the stated budget.
walkthrough: For hidden [0,1,3,4], n=4 and 2 is missing. At column 0, indices for values 0 and 4 have zero bits, while 1 and 3 have one bits. A tie selects missing bit 0 and keeps [0,4]. At column 1 both retained values have zero, so zeroCount>oneCount selects bit 1; the selected one partition is empty. Higher bits are zero, yielding binary 10 = 2.
timeComplexity: O(n) individual-bit queries and index-partition work across geometrically shrinking candidate sets; at most 32 bit positions in the fixed-width model.
spaceComplexity: O(n) auxiliary original-index lists; hidden integers are never reconstructed or copied into local numeric values.
edgeCases: Empty input, missing zero and missing n.
Shuffled values, boundaries around powers of two and n=10000.
Single-bit API index/column limits and the linear query budget.
